title: Knowledge-Building Helps Student Motivation, Too
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Following his argument that critical thinking is a function of knowledge, Stuart extends the idea to motivation. He restates his five beliefs behind student engagement (credibility, value, belonging, effort, efficacy) and compares two ninth-grade Algebra students, one with solid arithmetic foundations and one without. His claim is that prior knowledge feeds every belief: the student who follows the board work easily believes she can succeed and that she belongs, while the student with gaps doubts both, regardless of how warm her relationships are. The reframing is that many motivation problems are actually knowledge problems. That is good news, because the teacher's response becomes teaching rather than blaming, labeling or pathologizing the student.
points: Prior knowledge underlies the efficacy belief, since a student who already has the prerequisites will find it much easier to believe she can succeed.
Belonging is also knowledge-dependent: a student who cannot follow the work will doubt she fits in, even with strong peer and teacher relationships.
Diagnosing a motivation problem as a knowledge gap turns a vague character judgment into a concrete teaching task.
The post positions knowledge-building as a motivational strategy, not just an academic one.
quotes: Last time, I discussed how critical thinking is not the “holy grail” transferrable skill that we tend to think it is. Rather, it is a function of knowledge, something most deeply practicable in domains we know enough about.

When faced with a day’s lesson, who is going to find it easier to believe that they can succeed — all other things being equal? The Efficacy belief will be easier for Student A, simply because Student A is actually going to have a much easier time succeeding!

Conversely, Student B might have a wonderful relationship with the teacher and a great social connection with her peers, but when it’s time to get to the work of learning Algebra, she’s going to doubt whether or not she fits in with the rest of the class simply because she lacks the prior knowledge that the class requires.
Sometimes, the biggest motivational obstacle for the students in our classes is that they just don’t know enough. This lack of knowledge creates doubt and fear.

And this all sounds like bad news, but actually it’s the opposite. When we can identify that a student’s lack of motivation is stemming from a lack of prior knowledge, we now know exactly what we need to do next.
We don’t need to blame or label or pathologize the student. Instead, we can teach them.
